title: Basic Fluid Pressure
description: A draft pilot lesson for introductory pressure reasoning using source-linked structured content blocks.
learningOutcomes: Describe pressure as force distributed over area.
Identify the SI units used for pressure, force, and area.
Interpret a simple pressure result within stated educational assumptions.

blocks.text: This pilot lesson introduces pressure as a relationship between normal force and area for an introductory static-fluid context.
Students should be comfortable with basic algebra and SI units before attempting this lesson.
By the end of the lesson, students should be able to describe pressure, identify the units Pa, N, and m^2, and interpret a simple result within the stated limitations.
Pressure reasoning is used when engineers compare loads distributed over surfaces, interpret gauge readings, and recognise abnormal pressure conditions in supervised systems.

blocks.definition: Force distributed over an area in a fluid or on a surface.

blocks.title: Force distributed over area
blocks.altText: A downward force arrow spreads over a rectangular area, indicating pressure as force divided by area.
blocks.description: Force F acts normally on a surface area A. The larger the area for the same force, the lower the pressure.
blocks.caption: Concept diagram for introductory pressure reasoning.

blocks.text: For this introductory lesson, pressure is treated as normal force distributed across a stated area. The calculation is only meaningful when the quantities use consistent SI units.
The force is applied normally over the stated area, and the example is not a pressure-vessel design case.

blocks.note: Industrial Learn calculations store force in newtons, area in square metres, and pressure in pascals internally.

blocks.title: Pressure from a known force and area

steps.label: Check units
steps.expression: F in N, A in m^2
steps.explanation: Both quantities are already in the SI units used internally.

steps.label: Substitute values
steps.explanation: Use the source-linked pressure relationship from the equation block.

steps.label: Calculate pressure
steps.explanation: The pressure is expressed in pascals.

blocks.interpretation: A pressure of 400 Pa is the result for this educational example under the stated assumptions.

blocks.text: Simulation placeholder: adjust force and area in a future activity to observe pressure changes. No simulation state is implemented in this pilot lesson.

blocks.title: Unexpected pressure reading
symptoms: The reading is outside the expected training range.
likelyCauses: Sensor or gauge issue in a real system
blocks.safeResponse: Treat real-system abnormal pressure as a safety concern and follow supervised laboratory or site procedures.

blocks.title: Stored pressure
blocks.text: Real pressurised systems can be hazardous. This lesson does not authorise students to inspect, open, adjust, or operate pressurised equipment.

blocks.prompt: Which SI units should be used internally for the introductory pressure calculation in this lesson?
blocks.answerExplanation: The pilot lesson keeps force in N, area in m^2, and pressure in Pa.

blocks.text: Pressure is introduced here as force distributed over area. The pilot lesson keeps calculations in SI units and remains draft content until source and engineering review are complete.

blocks.note: OpenStax College Physics, section 11.3, supports the pressure definition, equation, and SI-unit relationship used in this draft. Independent educational, safety, and engineering review remain required before publication.
